title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: The artist Mihailov was, as always, at work when the cards of Count Vronsky and Golenishtchev were brought in. In the morning he had been working in his studio on his big picture. On getting home, he had flown into a rage with his wife for not having managed to fend off the landlady, who had been asking for money.

"I've told you twenty times — don't get into details with her. You're foolish enough at the best of times, and when you start explaining things in Italian you're three times the fool," he said after a long argument.
"Then don't let it run on so long; it's not my fault. If I had the money...."

"Leave me alone, for God's sake!" Mihailov shrieked, tears in his voice, and clapping his hands over his ears he stalked off into his workroom on the other side of a partition wall and shut the door behind him. "Idiotic woman!" he muttered to himself, sat down at the table, opened a portfolio, and at once set to work with peculiar intensity on a sketch he had started.

He never worked with such fervor and success as when things were going badly for him, and especially when he had quarreled with his wife. "Oh — the devil take them all!" he thought as he went on working. He was making a sketch for the figure of a man in a violent rage. There was an earlier version of it, but he had been dissatisfied with it. "No, that other one was better ... where is it?" He went back to his wife, and scowling, not looking at her, asked his eldest little girl where that piece of paper was that he had given them. The paper with the discarded sketch on it was found, but it was dirty, with candle-grease spots on it. Still, he took the sketch, laid it on his table, and, stepping back a little and screwing up his eyes, he fell to gazing at it. All at once he smiled and gestured gleefully.
"That's it! That's it!" he said, and at once picking up his pencil he began drawing rapidly. The spot of tallow had given the man a new pose.

He had sketched this new pose when all at once he remembered the face of a shopkeeper from whom he had bought cigars, a vigorous face with a prominent chin, and he sketched that very face, that very chin, onto the figure of the man. He laughed aloud with delight. From a lifeless thing of his imagination the figure had become alive, and become something that could never be changed. That figure was living, and was clearly and unmistakably defined. The sketch could be corrected to suit the demands of the figure — the legs, in fact, could and must be set differently, and the position of the left hand had to be entirely changed; the hair too could be thrown back. But in making those corrections he was not changing the figure but only stripping away what was hiding it. He was, in effect, peeling off the wrappings that kept it from being clearly seen. Each new touch only brought out the whole figure in all its force and vigor, as it had suddenly come to him from the spot of tallow. He was carefully finishing the figure when the cards were brought in to him.
He went in to his wife.

"Come, Sasha, don't be cross!" he said, smiling at her timidly and affectionately. "You were to blame. I was to blame. I'll make it all right." And having made peace with his wife, he put on an olive-green overcoat with a velvet collar and a hat, and headed for his studio. The successful figure he had already forgotten. Now he was delighted and excited at the visit of these people of consequence, Russians, who had come in their carriage.

About his picture — the one now standing on his easel — he had at the bottom of his heart one conviction: that no one had ever painted a picture like it. He did not believe his picture was better than all of Raphael's, but he knew that what he was trying to convey in that picture no one had ever conveyed. This he knew for certain, and had known for a long time — ever since he had begun painting it. But other people's criticisms, whatever they might be, still had enormous weight in his eyes, and they shook him to the depths of his soul. Any remark, even the most insignificant, that showed the critic had seen even the tiniest part of what he saw in the picture shook him to the depths of his soul. He always attributed to his critics a deeper understanding than he had himself, and always expected from them something he could not see in the picture himself. And often in their criticisms he imagined he had found just that.

He walked rapidly to the door of his studio, and despite his excitement was struck by the soft light on Anna's figure as she stood in the shade of the entrance listening to Golenishtchev, who was eagerly telling her something, while she clearly wanted to glance over at the artist. He was unconscious himself of how, as he approached them, he seized on this impression and absorbed it, just as he had the chin of the shopkeeper who had sold him the cigars, and stored it away somewhere to be brought out when he needed it. The visitors, not favorably predisposed beforehand by Golenishtchev's account of the artist, were even less so by his appearance. Thick-set and of middle height, with quick movements, in his brown hat, olive-green coat, and narrow trousers — even though wide trousers had long been in fashion — and, above all, with the ordinariness of his broad face and the mixed expression of timidity and anxious self-importance, Mihailov made an unpleasant impression.
"Please step in," he said, trying to look indifferent, and going into the passage he took a key out of his pocket and unlocked the door.
